tags.gist: Says Question 24 presumes manufacturers know which model their device uses; identifying the component should be a prerequisite to detecting change, not assumed done.
Says no manufacturer can detect changes in a component it has wrongly identified, since documentation drifts silently from deployment.
Reports the most consequential measured failure was upstream of the model, in audio capture, where model monitoring would not look.
Notes the failure left no log entry at all, so a monitoring program cannot see an event that the device never records.
Reports an automated reviewer confidently misread the failure's residue as the user simply stopping speaking.
Reports that on the commenter's own audited stack the code description named a local model while the code called a different vendor's hosted API.
Reports sample-level measurements showing audio capture, not the model, stopped delivering signal, with loss roughly doubling every forty minutes.
Reports a transcriber producing fluent words over dead input, and would extend element S.3 to false confidence about having received input.
Reports that terminated sessions and lost speech left zero log lines, so surveillance that assumes failures self-report will miss this class.
Reports a model reviewer inverting causation twice, and wants supervisory agents validated against failure residue that mimics normal use, without treating log agreement as corroboration.
Recommends a runtime component manifest emitted per inference by the calling path, stating the model, version and endpoint that actually served the output.
Would make version pinning a condition of clearance, with unpinned dependency itself a change and no PCCP for devices calling an unversioned endpoint.
Recommends input-integrity monitoring separate from model monitoring, verifying sensor or audio streams carry live signal and logging loss as an adverse event.
Wants absence of input, premature termination and dropped capture logged as rigorously as errors, since untraced failures escape every mechanism.
Proposes a benchmark element testing devices on inputs with no valid signal, with any fluent output scored as failure.
Calls contractual advance notice necessary but insufficient when component identity is not verifiable at runtime.
Says the failure was caught only because a sighted user watched the screen; a nonverbal user cannot contest a sentence invented in their name.
